claims.text: Chemically and electrochemically distinct phases in multiphase eutectic high-entropy alloys can produce localized galvanic cells.
The relevant multiphase microstructure can consist of an FCC matrix containing dispersed sigma phases.
Sigma-phase precipitates or comparable second phases are harder than the FCC matrix.
Friction can form an oxide film whose rupture leads to adhesive and abrasive wear.
At elevated temperature, wear repeatedly removes the protective oxide and exposes fresh alloy.
Potential differences between FCC and sigma phases cause galvanic corrosion.
Interphase boundaries specifically facilitate localized anodic dissolution after mechanical oxide removal.
Wear-induced oxide rupture and galvanic corrosion form a feedback loop that accelerates both wear and corrosion synergistically.
Post-solidification heat treatment or hot working can convert the eutectic alloy to a homogeneous single-phase structure without changing its overall composition.
The proposed controlled comparison holds bulk composition constant while varying the microstructure between multiphase and single-phase states.
A homogeneous single-phase alloy of the same composition will form a more uniform and stable passive oxide film and exhibit less galvanic coupling.
The multiphase alloy will have greater total degradation than the matched single-phase baseline.
The multiphase alloy will have a higher wear rate, greater material loss, and more pronounced wear scars than the single-phase baseline.
The multiphase alloy will exhibit accelerated corrosion, represented by a lower corrosion potential and a higher corrosion current density than the single-phase baseline.
The mechanism applies around 600 degrees Celsius during simultaneous sliding wear in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution.
The magnitude of the degradation increase depends strongly on phase morphology, phase distribution, and processing history.
Mass loss, wear-scar dimensions, friction coefficient, corrosion potential, current density, and impedance can be used to compare the two microstructures.
The hypothesis is falsified if the multiphase alloy does not show statistically significantly greater wear and accelerated corrosion than the matched single-phase alloy.
